# What `ndr()` estimates

Generalized network-based dimensionality reduction has three linked stages:

1. estimate or receive an association matrix;
2. detect communities in the squared-association network;
3. construct one standardized, centrality-weighted score per retained
   community.

Squaring lets community detection use relationship strength. The unsquared
association is retained for interpretation: positive edges are green,
negative edges are red, and absolute magnitude controls width. Community
membership is encoded by node colour only; indicators use one common shape by
default. This visual grammar remains feasible when a model contains many
communities.

<div class="visual-pipeline">
<div class="pipeline-step"><strong>Association</strong>Variables or observations become nodes.</div>
<div class="pipeline-step"><strong>Community</strong>Strongly connected nodes form modules.</div>
<div class="pipeline-step"><strong>Score</strong>Each retained module defines one latent score.</div>
</div>

# Full, partial, and semipartial networks

The association method and conditioning type are independent choices.
`cor_method` supports Pearson, Spearman, Kendall, distance, Gaussian-rank, and
biweight associations. `cor_type` supports full, partial, and semipartial
forms.

```{r association-comparison}
fit_full <- ndr(
  swiss, cor_method = "pearson", cor_type = "full",
  centrality = "pagerank", seed = 42
)
fit_partial <- ndr(
  swiss, cor_method = "pearson", cor_type = "partial",
  centrality = "pagerank", seed = 42
)
fit_semipartial <- ndr(
  swiss, cor_method = "pearson", cor_type = "semipartial",
  centrality = "authority", seed = 42
)

comparison <- data.frame(
  network = c("full", "partial", "semipartial"),
  factors = c(fit_full$factors, fit_partial$factors,
              fit_semipartial$factors),
  retained = c(sum(fit_full$membership > 0),
               sum(fit_partial$membership > 0),
               sum(fit_semipartial$membership > 0)),
  directed = c(fit_full$stats$directed,
               fit_partial$stats$directed,
               fit_semipartial$stats$directed)
)
comparison
```

Partial association asks whether two indicators remain related after the
others are controlled on both sides. Semipartial association controls one side
and may be directed; hub and authority centralities can therefore answer
different questions.

# Inspecting communities and latent scores

The full Pearson fit provides a compact example of the fitted object.

```{r inspect-fit}
fit_full
summary(fit_full)
fit_full$membership
round(fit_full$loadings, 3)
round(fit_full$communality, 3)
fit_full$stats$community_sizes
```

`membership` identifies the score to which an indicator contributes.
`loadings` connect indicators to the resulting scores; `communality` describes
how well each indicator is represented. A zero membership means exclusion.

For a confirmatory illustration, a fixed two-community structure makes the
network and biplot stable across community-detection backends.

```{r fixed-membership}
visual_fit <- ndr(
  swiss,
  cor_method = "pearson",
  membership = c(1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 0),
  centrality = "eigenvector",
  seed = 42
)
data.frame(
  indicator = colnames(visual_fit$R),
  community = unname(visual_fit$membership)
)
```

# Predicting new observations

```{r prediction}
new_scores <- predict(visual_fit, swiss[1:5, , drop = FALSE])
round(new_scores, 3)
identical(predict(visual_fit), visual_fit$scores)
```

Prediction reuses the training means, scales, indicator weights, centrality
weights, latent centring, latent scaling, and rotation. Consequently, scores
for new observations remain on the fitted model's coordinate system.

# Supplying an arbitrary matrix and clustering observations

With `covar = TRUE`, `ndr()` accepts a square matrix directly. This makes the
method usable beyond correlation matrices. The example below follows the
clustering use described in @Kosztyan2023: Euclidean distances between the
standardized Swiss observations are converted to similarities.

```{r observation-clustering}
scaled_swiss <- scale(swiss)
distance_matrix <- as.matrix(dist(scaled_swiss))
similarity_matrix <- 1 - normalize(distance_matrix)
diag(similarity_matrix) <- 1

cluster_fit <- ndr(
  similarity_matrix,
  covar = TRUE,
  min_comm = 2,
  centrality = "eigenvector",
  seed = 42
)
cluster_fit$factors
table(cluster_fit$membership)
head(cluster_fit$membership, 10)
is.null(cluster_fit$scores)
```

Here the nodes are observations rather than indicators. The returned
membership is therefore an observation clustering. Since an arbitrary matrix
contains no original row-level transformation, latent scores for new rows are
not available in this mode.

```{r clustering-network, fig.cap="Observation clusters obtained from a normalized Euclidean similarity matrix."}
cluster_network <- plot(
  cluster_fit,
  cuts = 0.55,
  interactive = FALSE,
  show_weights = FALSE,
  shape = "automatic",
  vertex.label.size = 7,
  layout = "fr"
)
cluster_network
```

# Static network and biplot

```{r ndr-static-network, fig.cap="NDR association network: colour denotes community, edge colour denotes sign, and width denotes absolute association."}
static_network <- plot(
  visual_fit,
  cuts = 0.3,
  interactive = FALSE,
  show_weights = TRUE,
  shape = "automatic"
)
static_network
```

All observed indicators use the same shape. The two communities differ only
by node colour. Solid green and red edges distinguish positive and negative
associations; their thickness is scaled between the requested minimum and
maximum widths.

```{r ndr-biplot, fig.cap="Two-factor NDR biplot for the fixed Swiss-data communities."}
score_biplot <- biplot(
  visual_fit,
  view_3D = FALSE,
  interactive = FALSE
)
score_biplot
```

Nearby observation points have similar score profiles. Loading arrows indicate
the direction of increasing indicator values. The graph explains association
structure; the biplot explains observations and indicators in latent-score
space. Neither should be read as a causal model.

# Inference, filtering, and weighting

The optional style controls can be demonstrated on the same fitted network.
All observed indicators remain rectangles, and community uses colour only.
Shapes are supplied in association-matrix column order.

```{r custom-network, fig.cap="Explicit common node shape, custom signed colours, and bounded edge widths."}
custom_network <- plot(
  visual_fit, interactive = FALSE,
  shape = rep("rectangle", ncol(visual_fit$R)),
  positive.color = "#007A53", negative.color = "#B71C1C",
  positive.lty = 1, negative.lty = 1,
  edge.width.range = c(1, 5), show_weights = TRUE
)
custom_network
```

For a four-node graph, an individual shape vector could instead be
`c("circle", "circle", "square", "square")`; shapes are not assigned by
community. Optional `positive.lty` and `negative.lty` control line types.
Both default to 1 (solid). Widths are scaled within the displayed graph;
separate graphs require a common scale for direct width comparisons.

Association tests and bootstrap intervals can be executed on a small example
without dominating build time. The low replicate count below illustrates the
returned structure; final inference should use a larger `n_boot`.

```{r inference}
inference_fit <- ndr(
  swiss,
  cor_method = "pearson",
  test = TRUE,
  p_adjust = "BH",
  alpha = 0.10,
  bootstrap = TRUE,
  n_boot = 30,
  conf = 0.90,
  seed = 42
)
round(inference_fit$correlation_p, 3)
head(inference_fit$stats$bootstrap$lower)
head(inference_fit$stats$bootstrap$upper)
```

The principal filtering controls are `min_R`, `min_evalue`,
`min_communality`, `com_communalities`, and `min_comm`. The `weight` argument
supplies one finite score weight per indicator. These filters act at different
stages: network formation, centrality screening, representation, loading
separation, and minimum module size.

# Sparse storage and reproducible settings

```{r sparse-fit}
sparse_fit <- ndr(
  swiss,
  min_R = 0.15,
  sparsecalc = TRUE,
  seed = 42
)
inherits(sparse_fit$R, "sparseMatrix")
sparse_fit$factors
sparse_fit$stats$community_sizes
```

Sparse storage is helpful after thresholding a large network. Parallel workers
mainly benefit pairwise distance association and bootstrap calculations; small
Pearson examples usually run faster sequentially. A fixed `seed` makes the
stochastic parts reproducible.
